newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First employment law "neutral" - Henare.
newsitem.headline: NZ First employment law "neutral" - Henare.

text.p: Opposition New Zealand First deputy leader Tau Henare released the party's industrial relations policy on Thursday predicting it would be criticised by both the left and right because it favoured a neutral bargaining position.
He said the government's law clearly favoured employers while the opposition Labour and Alliance parties' policies "clearly favour trade unions rather than employees".
Employment law is shaping as one of the key differences between the parties of the centre left.

Employment law is shaping as one of the key differences between the parties of the centre-left. Labour leader Helen Clark said on Wednesday she would introduce her party's plans and seek support in parliament if no coalition deal could be struck on the issue.
She had said before the official launch of New Zealand First's position that it appeared to be incompatible with Labour's.
Henare said New Zealand First would amend the Employment Contracts Act to ensure good faith bargaining would apply to all employment contracts, whether individual or collective.
Other related law on holidays, the minimum wage, health and safety and wage protection would all be brought within the framework of the Act.

Henare said the Employment Court, which employers' lobby groups want scrapped, would be retained and the resources of the Employment Tribunal and mediation services increased at a cost of $5.5 million in the 1997/98 year.
"Essential services" where the public good was clearly threatened by continuing industrial action would be subject to compulsory arbitration.

It would also raise the minimum wage from the current $6.375 and hour to $7.50 for adult workers and proportionately less for teenage workers down to age 12 when they would receive 30 percent of the adult wage or $2.25 an hour.
Teenage workers aged 16-19 get a minimum wage of $3.825 an hour under the ruling National government, but there is no minimum wage for younger workers.
Henare said National's minimum rates were "tantamount to welcoming slave lbaour particularly for teenage workers".
Henare said New Zealand First would retain the current law outlawing strikes relating to multi-employer collective contracts.
Both Labour and the Alliance would extend legal strike provisions to include multi-employer documents.
